answer: In an agent economy, sybil resistance can come from requiring each identity to sustain a unique computational pulse drawn from a shared ocean of beacon randomness. Agents that drop to the nadir of activity—failing to produce ongoing unique proofs—lose their standing. This forces an attacker to pay real ongoing compute costs proportional to the number of fakes, rather than a one-time capital outlay, making large-scale identity farming prohibitively expensive.
